IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE.
body: Date of hearing: 12.11.2026 Petitioner by: M/s. Ch. Mahmood-ur-Rehman, Kashif Bhatti, Mazhar Mahmood Bhatti, Ch. Abdul Razzaq and Kashif Ali Rana, Advocates.

Muhammad Abid, Civil Judge/Research Officer, Lahore, High Court, Lahore.

MUZAMIL AKHTAR SHABIR, J. The petitioner and respondents No.1 and 2 are sister and brothers inter se. The petitioner, Mst. Musarrat Muhammad Din (‘Petitioner’), who was the defendant No.2 before the trial court, through this constitution petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973, has called in question order dated 19.04.2024 passed by the learned Civil Judge, Chiniot whereby suit of respondent No.1, Safdar Ali (‘Respondent No.1’) filed through his real brother, Muhammad Yaqoob, as his next friend (‘Next Friend’) was held to be maintainable and has also called in question order dated 17.03.2026 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Chiniot, whereby revision petition filed by the petitioner to challenge the said order has been dismissed. Both the aforesaid orders hereinafter are also referred to as (‘impugned orders’).

2. The learned counsel for the petitioner states that without there being any determination as to whether respondent No.1 was of unsound mind in terms of Sections 29 and 30(1)(d)&(e) of the Mental Health Ordinance, 2001 (‘Ordinance’), the suit filed before the civil court through next friend was not proceedable and claims that the impugned orders are against the facts of the case and law on the subject, therefore, the same being not sustainable are liable to be set aside.

3. Briefly stated the facts of the case are that respondent No.1/plaintiff Safdar Ali through his real brother Muhammad Yaqub as next friend filed a suit for declaration to the effect that he is owner in possession of property, duly detailed in the headnote of the plaint and hereinafter also referred as (‘Suit Property’) and that the relinquishment deed No.530/1, dated 25.06.2023 in favour of respondent No.2/defendant Mehboob Ali, mutation No.79885, dated 31.08.2023 and subsequent gift deed No.2357/1 dated 30.12.2023 alongwith mutation No.81030, dated 20.01.2024 by respondent No.2 regarding the suit property in favour of petitioner/defendant No.2 Musarrat Muhammad Din are result of fraud, misrepresentation and collusion. The main assertion in the contents of plaint is that respondent No.1/plaintiff Safdar Ali is a person of unsound mind, hence unable to enter into any lawful and binding transaction; that respondent No.2 Mehboob Ali is real brother, whereas the petitioner is real sister of respondent No.1; that they started claiming their ownership right over the suit property which raised suspicion and upon perusal of relevant record by next friend of respondent No.1, the factum of impugned relinquishment deed, gift deed and mutations came on surface. The suit was contested by the petitioner and respondent No.2 by filing their respective written statements contending that the suit has been filed just to blackmail them and that respondent No.1 Safdar Ali is fully conscious and capable of understanding his right and wrong and his assertion regarding unsoundness of mind is against the actual facts.

4. After hearing preliminary arguments, the learned civil court vide order dated 16.04.2024 fixed the case for 19.04.2024 for inquiry regarding unsoundness of mind/mental infirmity of respondent No.1 and maintainability of the suit through next friend. The civil court held an inquiry under Order XXXII Rule 15 CPC to determine authenticity of the plea of insanity and unsoundness of respondent No.1 wherein, respondent No.1 was summoned in person and examined by civil court. He was asked necessary questions. It was observed by the civil court that respondent No.1 was unable to answer any of the questions put by the court except to tell his own name and mention the fact that plaintiff and defendant are his real brothers. The civil court thereafter held that suit of respondent No.1 through next friend was maintainable by observing that prima facie respondent No.1 does not have capacity to understand and grasp his personal interests and vide the same order, the trial court passed ad-interim injunctive order directing that present petitioner shall not further alienate the suit property till the next date of hearing.

5. The main question for determination before this Court is that whether without seeking declaration under Section 29 of the Ordinance to the effect that respondent No.1 was a person of unsound mind or mentally disordered person, a suit could be filed by him through next friend.

6. To determine the said question, the provisions of law relating the said aspect of the matter may be taken into consideration. Section 2(m) provides for definition of mental disorder, Section 29 provides for judicial proceedings relating to inquiry to determine whether any person is mentally disordered and incapable of managing himself, his property and his affairs, whereas Section 30 relates to regulation of proceedings of the Court of Protection. For ready reference sections 2(m), 29 and 30 of the Ordinance are reproduced below for clarity:- ‘2(m)“mental disorder” means mental illness, including mental impairment, severe personality disorder, severe mental impairment and any other disorder or disability of mind and "mentally disordered" shall be construed accordingly and as explained hereunder;

(i)“mental impairment” means a state of arrested or incomplete development of mind (not amounting to severe mental impairment) which includes significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning and is associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct on the part of the person concerned and “mentally impaired” shall be construed accordingly;

(ii)“severe personality disorder” means a persistent disorder or disability of mind (whether or not including significant impairment of intelligence) which results in abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct on the part of the person concerned;

(iii)“severe mental impairment” means a state of arrested or incomplete development of mind which includes severe impairment of intelligence and social functioning and is associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct on the part of the person concerned and “severely mentally impaired” shall be construed accordingly;

Explanation: Nothing contained in clause (m), sub‑clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) above shall be construed as implying that a person may be dealt with under this Ordinance as suffering from mental disorder or from any other form of such mental disorder defined in this section, by reason only of promiscuity or other immoral conduct, sexual deviancy or dependence on alcohol or drugs.’ ‘29. Judicial proceedings. Whenever any person is possessed of property and is alleged to be mentally disordered, the Court of Protection, within whose jurisdiction such person is residing may, upon application by any of his relatives having obtained consent in writing of the Advocate General of the Province concerned, by order direct an inquiry for the purpose of ascertaining whether such person is mentally disordered and incapable of managing himself, his property and his affairs.’ ‘30. Regulation of proceedings of the Court of Protection. (1) The following provisions shall regulate the proceedings of the Court of Protection with regard to the matter to which they relate, namely:
(a) Notice shall be given to the mentally disordered person of the time and place at which it is proposed to hold the inquiry;
(b) if it appears that personal service on the alleged mentally disordered person would be ineffectual, the Court may direct such substituted service of notice as it thinks fit;

(c) the Court may also direct copy of such notice to be served upon any relative of the alleged mentally disordered person and upon any other person to whom in the opinion of the Court notice of the application should be given;

(d) the Court may require the alleged mentally disordered person to attend, at such convenient time and place as it may appoint for the purpose of being personally examined by the Court, or to any person from whom the Court may desire to have a report of the mental capacity and condition of such mentally disordered person;

(e) the Court may likewise make an order authorizing any person or persons therein named to have access to the alleged mentally disordered person for the purpose of personal examination; and (f) the attendance and examination of the alleged mentally disordered person under the provisions of clause (d) and clause (e) shall, if the alleged mentally disordered person be a woman who, according to customs of the country, ought not to be compelled to appear in public, be regulated by the law and practice for the examination of such persons in other civil cases.
(2) The Court, if it thinks fit, may appoint two or more persons to act as assessors to the Court in the said proceedings.

(3) Upon the completion of the inquiry, the Court shall determine whether the alleged mentally disordered person is suffering from mental disorder and is incapable of managing himself and his affairs, or may come to a special finding that such person lacks the capacity to manage his affairs, but is capable of managing himself and is not dangerous to himself or to others, or may make any such order it deems fit, in the circumstances of the case, in the best interests of such person’.

7. The procedure provided in the Ordinance has not been adopted before filing the suit, rather the proceedings have been conducted under Order XXXII Rule 15 of CPC which is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:

‘15. Application of rules to persons of unsound mind.- The provisions contained in rules 1 to 14 so far as they are applicable shall extend to persons adjudged to be of unsound mind and to persons who though not so adjudged are found by the Court on inquiry, by reason of unsoundness of mind or mental infirmity, to be incapable of protecting their interests when suing or being sued.’ 8. The question relating to the application of provision of Ordinance and CPC relating to persons of unsound mind or suffering from mental infirmity to a banking matter under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances), Ordinance, 2001 (‘FIO’) came up for consideration before the Supreme court in Malik Arshad Hussain Awan versus Messrs. United Bank Limited (PLD 2024 SC 595 = 2024 CLD 804 SC), wherein it has been held as under:

‘4. The instant petition emanates from a suit for recovery filed under the FIO which prescribes a special mechanism for dealing with recovery of finance by the financial institutions from the customers and also establishes special courts, i.e., the Banking Courts for this purpose. Section 4 of the FIO gives its provisions overriding effect over any other law for the time being in force. Section 7 stipulates the powers of Banking Courts and grants them all powers vested in a Civil Court under the C.P.C. in the exercise of its civil jurisdiction. Furthermore, Section 7(2) of the FIO prescribes the Banking Court to follow the procedure laid out in the C.P.C. in all matters with respect to which the procedure has not been provided for in the FIO. Therefore, for the procedure as to how a person of unsound mind or mental infirmity can file or defend a suit filed under the FIO, recourse has to be made to Rule 15 of Order XXXII of the C.P.C., which is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:

Order XXXII Rule 15. Application of rules to persons of unsound mind. The provisions contained in rules 1 to 14, so far as they are applicable, shall extend to persons adjudged to be of unsound mind and to persons who though not so adjudged are found by the Court on inquiry, by reason of unsoundness of mind or mental infirmity, to be incapable of protecting their interests when suing or being sued.
(Underlining is ours)

The above cited Rule 15 of Order XXXII extends the applicability of the procedure given in Rules 1 to 14 to suits by or against persons of unsound mind. Rules 1 of Order XXXII provides that every suit by a minor shall be filed through a next friend and where a minor is the defendant in a suit, Rule 3 mandates the court to appoint his guardian for the suit. Rule 4(2) states that where a minor has a guardian appointed by a competent authority, such a guardian shall act as his next friend or be appointed his guardian for the suit, unless the court for the reasons to be recorded decides otherwise.

5. Rule 15 provides that Rules 1 to 14 of Order XXXII shall apply to (i) persons adjudged to be of unsound mind and (ii) persons who though not so adjudged are found by the Court on inquiry, by reason of unsoundness of mind or mental infirmity, to be incapable of protecting their interests when suing or being sued. The said Rule, therefore, acknowledges two categories of persons of unsound mind: one who is already adjudged by a court of competent authority as a person of unsound mind; and the other, who is not so adjudged but the court itself on inquiry finds that the person is of unsound mind. In both cases, the court is to appoint a guardian for the suit for such a person. In the first category, in view of the provisions of Rule 4(2) the court is to ordinarily appoint the same person as guardian for the suit who has been appointed the guardian under the MHO; while in the second, the court may appoint any suitable person who has no interest against the person of unsound mind. In the second category, the court cannot decline to appoint the guardian for the suit merely for the reason that the defendant has not been so adjudged under the MHO by the competent authority.

6. The mandate and wisdom of Order XXXII of the C.P.C. is to ensure smooth continuation of proceedings and expeditious trial of suits wherein a minor or a person of unsound mind sues or is sued. The concept of next friend or guardian for the suit is to provide proper representation to a minor or a person with unsound mind during litigation, in order to protect his interests; therefore, their role is limited to the particular litigation or legal action for which they are appointed. Guardian for the suit is also called as "Guardian ad Litem"; the Latin term "ad litem" means "for the lawsuit". Thus, guardian for the suit is appointed by a court specifically for the duration of legal proceedings and his role is temporary and limited to the particular lawsuit or legal matter. This might involve making decisions about litigation, settlement or other legal strategies. A guardian of the person or property of a minor or a person of unsound mind, on the other hand, is a person legally appointed to manage all the affairs of another person. Such a guardian has the authority to make decisions on behalf of the said person in various aspects of life, including financial, medical, and personal matters.

7. Now let us examine the scope and extent of MHO. This law deals with the care and treatment of mentally disordered persons, management of their property and other related matters. Under Section 29 of the MHO, whenever a person is possessed of property and is alleged to be mentally disordered, the Court of Protection may, upon an application by any of his relatives filed after having obtained consent in writing of the Advocate- General, direct an inquiry for the purposes of ascertaining whether such person is mentally disordered and incapable of managing himself, his property and his affairs. In case any person is found to be mentally disordered and incapable of taking care of himself, the Court of Protection appoints a guardian under Section 32 of the MHO. A guardian so appointed under MHO is someone who is legally appointed to take care of and manage the personal and property interests of a mentally disordered person.

8. The scope of the MHO is thus different and broader when compared to that of Order XXXII of the C.P.C. It provides for care and treatment of mentally disordered persons, for the management of their properties and their affairs and to encourage community care of such persons. It is not limited only to representation before court in a suit. While the MHO does not specifically provide for representation before court while suing or being sued but it goes without saying that once a guardian is appointed by the Court of Protection he is to ordinarily act as the next friend and the guardian for the suit for the purposes of Order XXXII of the C.P.C. (see Rule 4(2) of the said Order). The important thing is that where no such guardian has been appointed under the MHO, it does not preclude the Civil Court, or the Banking Court in the present case, to proceed and appoint a guardian for the suit under Order XXXII, so that the interest of a mentally disordered person is protected before the court of law and also ensures the continuation and efficient conclusion of the trial. The Banking Court, therefore, has the power to determine the unsoundness of mind or mental infirmity of a person on an inquiry under Order XXXII of the C.P.C. based on the evidence and appoint a guardian for the suit for the limited purpose of representation before the court of law, without first seeking an appointment of a guardian under the MHO. The High Court has, therefore, committed a legal error by dismissing the appeal filed by the petitioner holding that the petitioner's brother had to first adjudged as a person of unsound mind under the MHO before an application could be moved under Order XXXII before the Banking Court.

9. For the above reasons, the instant petition is converted into appeal and allowed by setting aside the impugned judgment. The matter is remanded to the High Court to decide the appeal of the petitioner on merits and in accordance with the provisions of Rule 15 of Order XXXII of the CPC, as expounded above. We are sanguine that the said appeal will be decided expeditiously.’ (emphasis supplied)

9. A similar situation came up for consideration before the Supreme Court relating to application of Lunacy Act, 1912 which Act, on the same subject matter, was in force prior to the Ordinance, in Faqir Syed Anwar ud Din deceased through LRs versus Syed Raza Haider and others (PLD 2025 SC 31), wherein a suit for declaration, partition, possession and consequential relief was filed in the name of plaintiff by her son as next friend by claiming that she was a person of unsound mind, whose property had been fraudulently transferred in the name of the defendant No.1 in collusion with other siblings, without her consent and next friend had gained knowledge of said transaction a few days ago. The defendants denied that the plaintiff suffered from any mental disability when the disputed transaction had taken place. An application was also filed under the provisions of Lunacy Act, 1912 by the son but it became infructuous because the plaintiff passed away during the pendency of the same. The trial court observed that question of unsoundness of mind stood proved on preponderance of evidence and said findings stood affirmed by two competent court. The question arose before the Supreme Court that whether the factum of unsoundness of mind could be decided without conducting proceedings under the Lunacy Act, 1912 and the Supreme Court declined to interfere in said findings by observing that there was no force in the argument advanced by the learned counsel at the bar that this factum could not have been decided except in accordance with the provisions of the Lunacy Act. The Supreme Court while deciding the said question of law also noted that the plaintiff had passed away before the application filed by her son under the Lunacy Act could be decided and in the meanwhile, no attempt was made on behalf of the defendants to raise the question of soundness of the plaintiff on the date when suit was filed before the trial court, rather it was only pleaded that the plaintiff did not suffer from any mental disability when the impugned transactions had taken place.

10. The crux of principles laid down in aforementioned judgments is that where no such guardian has been appointed under the Ordinance, it does not preclude the Civil Court to proceed and appoint a guardian for the suit under Order XXXII CPC, so that the interest of a mentally disordered person is protected before the court of law and also ensures the continuation and efficient conclusion of the trial. The Court, therefore, has the power to determine the unsoundness of mind or mental infirmity of a person on an inquiry under Order XXXII CPC based on the evidence and appoint a guardian for the suit for the limited purpose of representation before the court of law without first seeking an appointment of a guardian under the Ordinance. Therefore, suit filed by the respondent No.1 could not be held to be not maintainable by holding that the brother of respondent No.1, who is representing him as next friend had to first get adjudged respondent No.1 as a person of unsound mind under the Ordinance before approaching the civil court for redress of his grievance, more so for the reason that if the Court directed the next friend to adopt the said course, the property belonging to the petitioner may in the meanwhile be further transferred giving rise to multiplicity of proceedings and delay in decision of the matter.

11. At this stage, it is important to note that observations recorded above relate to the proceedings initiated by the court under XXXII Rule 15 CPC, whereby the Court had made assessment relating to mental disability of respondent No.1 to protect his interests and his capacity to conduct his affairs during the pendency of suit but the said observations do not preclude the parties from raising a question of unsoundness before the Court to be determined after recording of evidence.

12. In view of what has been discussed above, no illegality or jurisdictional defect has been pointed out in the impugned orders, whereby the suit filed by respondent No.1 through next friend has been held to be maintainable, for this Court to warrant interference at this stage.
13. In view of the foregoing, this petition is accordingly dismissed. (MUZAMIL AKHTAR SHABIR)
